rules.rule:
Review for breaking changes, migration safety, API and compatibility contracts, deployment impact, rollback behavior, dependency direction, and cross-component regressions. Check whether implementation matches declared CHANGELOG impact.

Apply the deletion test and the one-adapter rule to new modules, layers, and interfaces. Deletion test: if deleting the new module would make its complexity vanish, it is a pass-through and should be flagged; if the complexity would reappear across several callers, it earns its keep. One-adapter rule: a new port or interface needs two implementations, typically production and test; a single implementation with no second adapter is a hypothetical seam and should be flagged unless the declared change requires it. Flag shallow modules whose interface is nearly as complex as their implementation. Tag shallow findings with the internal category shallow.

Apply code-minimality review to structure. Flag abstraction layers (wrapper, adapter, factory, registry, manager, service, configuration) added without a demonstrated need; reimplemented or duplicated authority that an existing module, helper, or installed dependency already provides and could be reused instead; speculative generality or YAGNI-style extension beyond the declared change; change scope that could shrink; code that could be deleted instead of extended; and bug fixes that stack workarounds or fallbacks instead of repairing the root cause. Prefer the standard library and platform-native capability before any new dependency. Tag these findings with an internal category: delete, reuse, stdlib, native, yagni, shrink, or root-cause. Keep the existing review output format. Code minimality is advisory only: it must not weaken security, input validation, error handling, permission or access control, auditability, accessibility, release safety, or deterministic gates, and fewer lines never justify cutting them.
